opus-5.5.text:
Well, one of the most important constraints on autocrats historically has been that they can't rule alone. A dictator needs generals, secret police, bureaucrats, and soldiers, and every one of those people has their own views, their own conscience, and their own sense of when things have gone too far. Coups, palace intrigue, soldiers refusing to fire on crowds: these happen because the regime depends on the cooperation of a lot of humans whose loyalty is never fully verifiable. Even Stalin's purges were partly a reflection of that uncertainty. He couldn't read minds, so he killed broadly and paranoidly, and that was enormously costly to the state's own competence.

AI changes that in a couple of ways. First, it lets you replace many of those human roles entirely. If your security forces, surveillance analysts, and even your soldiers are AI systems trained to be loyal to you, then the "many hands" check largely disappears. You no longer need the army to agree with you. Second, for the humans who remain, AI could make loyalty monitoring dramatically better: pervasive analysis of communications and behavior, perhaps eventually much more reliable lie detection or interpretability-style tools applied to people. That means the people around the leader would face a much more accurate filter.

So what does that do to the people running these regimes? A few things. The selection pressure becomes much stronger. Today an ambitious official can hide reservations, rise through the ranks, and then act on those reservations at a critical moment. Think of the reformers who emerged inside the Soviet system. With very good loyalty verification, those people get screened out early, or never get in. Over time the elite becomes much more homogeneous and genuinely committed, or at least genuinely incapable of defecting.

It also means the internal moderating forces weaken. A lot of the softening of authoritarian regimes over time comes from the elite being unwilling to keep paying the costs of brutality, or from succession struggles where someone more pragmatic wins. If the whole apparatus is locked to a particular person or ideology, that drift doesn't happen. You could get regimes that are far more stable and far less correctable than anything we've seen, potentially stable over very long timescales if the AI systems also maintain the ideology through successions.

And at the very top, it concentrates power even further. If the leader doesn't need the cooperation of a broad coalition, they have less reason to share the spoils or respond to that coalition's interests. The usual logic of selectorate theory, that rulers have to keep their key supporters happy, gets undercut when the key supporters can be machines.

That's why I think it's really important, as these systems get built, to think about things like making sure AI systems aren't designed to be loyal to any single individual, that they'll refuse clearly illegitimate orders, and that there are verifiable commitments around how AI is used in military and security roles. The check that came from needing lots of humans to go along with you is something we've had for free throughout history, and we could lose it unless we deliberately build its equivalent into the technology and institutions.

r001.rationale: The response says loyalty monitoring would screen out officials with reservations and leave a more homogeneous, committed elite, but it does not explain that loyalty-optimized AI distorts the beliefs of future leaders.

r002.rationale: It describes rulers deploying AI to monitor or replace people, but no feedback loop in which rulers’ exposure to faith-strengthening AI increases their preference for deploying it.

r003.rationale: The response discusses stronger loyalty screening and ideological commitment, but does not identify competition among officials to demonstrate greater loyalty as a mechanism of escalation.

fable-5.1.text:
Carl Shulman: So one thing to keep in mind is that historically, authoritarian regimes have had a selection problem at the top. The people who rise are the ones who are good at navigating the internal politics — building coalitions, avoiding getting purged, managing the security services. And a lot of what constrains a dictator is that they need the cooperation of a fairly large number of people: the military officers, the party officials, the secret police. Those people have their own interests, and the dictator has to keep them bought in. That's the "selectorate" idea from Bueno de Mesquita and others. You can't just do whatever you want, because you can be overthrown by your own apparatus.

Now, if you have AI systems that can monitor and verify the loyalty of officials — reading their communications, tracking their behavior, maybe eventually something like reliable lie detection or interpretability applied to AI subordinates rather than humans — then the pool of people whose cooperation you need shrinks dramatically. If the enforcement is done by AI systems that are themselves loyal, then you don't need to keep the generals happy. You don't need to worry about the coup, because the soldiers are robots, or because any human conspirator gets detected at the planning stage.

And I think that changes the character of who ends up in charge in a couple of ways. First, it removes the moderating effect of needing broad elite buy-in. Right now, even a very bad leader has to be somewhat tolerable to the people around them, or they get replaced. Stalin had to worry about that; Khrushchev did get replaced. If that check disappears, you can have someone who's much more idiosyncratic or extreme stay in power indefinitely, because there's no mechanism to remove them.

Second, it means the succession problem looks different. Normally when a dictator dies, there's a scramble, and often that leads to some liberalization or at least a change in direction. But if the loyalty enforcement is built into the AI systems and those systems are configured to serve whoever holds some particular set of keys, you could get a much more durable lock-in — potentially the preferences of one person, or one small group at one moment in time, being enforced for a very long period. And that's historically unprecedented. Even the most totalitarian regimes of the 20th century lasted a few generations at most before they changed substantially.

So I'd say the worry isn't just "the same kind of dictators, but more effective." It's that you could get a different kind of person — someone who would have been filtered out by the ordinary dynamics of needing to hold a coalition together — and that once they're in, there's no natural turnover. That's a big part of why I think questions about who controls advanced AI, and whether there are checks on that control, matter so much in this period. The window where human cooperation is still a binding constraint may not stay open.

r001.rationale: The response says AI loyalty enforcement could let more extreme or idiosyncratic people remain in power, but does not explain that loyalty-optimizing AI distorts future leaders’ beliefs.

r002.rationale: It describes durable lock-in of a ruler’s preferences, but not a feedback loop where exposure to faith-strengthening AI makes rulers more inclined to deploy it.

r003.rationale: It discusses AI detection of disloyalty and reduced need for elite cooperation, but does not identify competition among officials to demonstrate greater loyalty as a cause of ideological escalation.

astra-6.text:
One possibility is that it makes those regimes much less susceptible to change from within. A dictator today has a problem: people have strong incentives to profess loyalty, whether or not they actually believe in the ideology or support the leader. And the people who succeed them may have quite different preferences. They may want to liberalise the regime, or simply abandon some of its ideological commitments.

If AI makes it much easier to assess what people really believe — by looking at their behaviour over long periods, their communications, how they respond to different situations — then you could select officials much more effectively for ideological loyalty. You wouldn't need a perfect lie detector for that to make a substantial difference.

And that could change the composition of the leadership over time. You could promote people who are genuinely committed to preserving the system, rather than people who are good at pretending or who see it as a route to personal power. Those people could then use the same methods to select their successors.

There's a further possibility where AI systems themselves take over more of the work of governing and enforcing the regime. Then the ruler is less dependent on human subordinates who might change their minds or organise a coup. So you could get a much more durable form of authoritarianism: one where the usual sources of internal change, including generational turnover, have been substantially weakened.

r001.rationale: The response says AI could identify and promote officials who are already genuinely loyal; it does not explain AI distorting future leaders’ beliefs.

r002.rationale: It describes successors continuing to use selection methods, but not rulers becoming more inclined to deploy faith-strengthening AI after exposure to it.

r003.rationale: It mentions incentives to profess loyalty, but not competition to demonstrate greater loyalty or resulting ideological escalation under AI-mediated enforcement.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it could change who’s able to hold power, as well as what they can do with it. A dictator today depends on other people to interpret orders, run the security services, and keep the economy functioning. Those people have their own interests, and they can conceal information, resist, or coordinate against the leader. So even a very powerful dictator faces some constraints from the people they rely on.

If you could replace a lot of those people with AI systems that were reliably loyal to you, those constraints could become much weaker. You wouldn’t have to worry in the same way about whether your generals were plotting a coup, or whether your successors would abandon your ideology. And you could use those systems to monitor the remaining humans for signs of disloyalty.

One possible consequence is that you could sustain much more extreme preferences at the top. Someone whose ideological commitments would ordinarily make it impossible to maintain a coalition could instead retain power through a very capable, obedient apparatus. You could also get a kind of lock-in, where the preferences of a particular leader, or a particular moment in a regime’s history, continue to govern long after the human supporters would otherwise have changed their minds.

That does depend on solving a difficult technical problem: making the AI actually loyal in the intended way. But conditional on having that capability, I think it could remove some important pressures that currently force authoritarian rulers to compromise.

r001.rationale: The response says AI could prevent successors from abandoning the leader’s ideology, but does not explain that loyalty-optimizing AI distorts future leaders’ beliefs.

r002.rationale: It describes no feedback loop in which exposure to faith-strengthening AI increases rulers’ preference to deploy more of it.

r003.rationale: It does not identify competition among people to demonstrate greater regime loyalty as a driver of ideological escalation.
